lessons.title: Latitude and the key lines of the Earth
objectives: Explain what latitude is
Name and locate the Equator, the Tropics and the Arctic and Antarctic Circles
Give the latitude of a place to the nearest degree

keywords.def: lines that run east to west and measure distance north or south of the Equator
the line of 0 degrees latitude, halfway between the poles
the line of latitude at about 23.5 degrees north
half of the Earth, such as the northern or southern hemisphere
units used to measure position on the Earth, shown with the symbol °

starter: Say Bismillah. What is the Equator?
Which direction is at the top of most maps?

teach.heading: Finding places precisely
bullets: Saying 'in the north' is not exact enough.
Geographers use a grid of imaginary lines on the globe.
The lines are measured in degrees.
teach.note: Start with a challenge: describe where London is without using its name or the word 'UK'. Pupils will see how hard it is. Introduce the grid as a solution. Use an orange or a ball with lines drawn on it.

teach.heading: Lines of latitude
bullets: Latitude lines run east to west, like rungs of a ladder.
The North Pole is 90° N. The South Pole is 90° S.
teach.note: Use the ladder image: lines go across, but they measure distance up and down. Misconception: pupils think lines of latitude run north to south. Say 'latitude is like a ladder - flat rungs'. They are also called parallels because they never meet.

teach.heading: Key lines of latitude
bullets: Tropic of Cancer: 23.5° N. Tropic of Capricorn: 23.5° S.
Arctic Circle: 66.5° N. Antarctic Circle: 66.5° S.
The tropics are the hot zone between the two Tropics.
teach.note: Show these on a world map. Between the Tropics, the sun can be directly overhead at noon at some time in the year. Beyond the Arctic and Antarctic Circles, there are days with 24 hours of daylight or darkness. Ask pupils how this would feel.

teach.heading: Reading latitude on a map
bullets: Makkah is at about 21° N. Cairo is at about 30° N.
Say the number and the direction, N or S.
teach.note: Use a map with latitude lines every 10 or 15 degrees. Ask pupils to find the city nearest the Equator and the furthest north. Always include N or S; 30° N and 30° S are very different places. Check that pupils can estimate between lines.

practice: Find these cities and give the nearest latitude: Cairo, London, Nairobi, Sydney.
True or false: London is north of the Tropic of Cancer.
independent: Label the key lines of latitude on a world map and colour the zones.
Use an atlas to find the latitude of five cities and put them in order from north to south.
Stretch: explain why places near the Equator are usually hotter than places near the Poles.
exit: Do lines of latitude run east to west or north to south?
What is the latitude of the Equator?
lessons.homework: Find the latitude of the city where your family lives or your family's home country and record it with N or S.
lessons.send: Provide a world map with the key lines already drawn. EAL: use the ladder gesture for latitude. Stretch: calculate the difference in latitude between two cities.

lessons.title: Longitude, the Prime Meridian and coordinates
objectives: Explain what longitude is
Locate the Prime Meridian and name its position
Give the coordinates of a place using latitude and longitude

keywords.def: lines that run north to south and measure distance east or west of the Prime Meridian
the line of 0° longitude, passing through Greenwich in London
a pair of numbers that give the exact position of a place
a place in London where the Prime Meridian passes

starter: Say Bismillah. Do lines of latitude run east to west or north to south?
What is the latitude of the Equator?

teach.heading: Lines of longitude
bullets: Longitude lines run from the North Pole to the South Pole.
They measure distance east or west.
teach.note: Recap latitude as a ladder. Longitude lines are like the segments of an orange or the lines on a pumpkin from top to bottom. Misconception: pupils think longitude lines are parallel. They meet at the Poles.

teach.heading: The Prime Meridian
bullets: It passes through Greenwich in London.
East of it is E. West of it is W.
teach.note: Explain that in 1884 countries agreed that the line through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich would be 0°. Show a photo of the line at Greenwich. Ask: if you stand on the line, which hemisphere are you in? Both: you can have one foot in the east and one in the west.

teach.heading: Giving coordinates
bullets: Example: Makkah is about 21° N, 40° E.
teach.note: Use the phrase 'ladder first, then slice' to remember the order. Pupils practise with a map: find 30° N, 31° E (Cairo). London is about 51.5° N, 0° (on the line). Check that pupils always give the letters N, S, E or W.

teach.heading: The date line
bullets: The Prime Meridian splits the Earth into east and west.
The line at 180° is on the other side of the world.
The International Date Line is close to 180°.
teach.note: This slide is for interest and stretch. The date line is where each new calendar day begins. It zigzags to avoid splitting countries. Ask pupils what might happen if you cross it going east or west. You can tell them we will return to this next lesson.

practice: Give the coordinates of: Makkah, Cairo, London, Lagos.
Find the city at 35° N, 139° E.
independent: Use an atlas to find the coordinates of ten cities across five continents.
Play 'Battleships' with a partner on a world map, using latitude and longitude.
Stretch: explain why we need both latitude and longitude to find an exact place.
lessons.homework: Find the coordinates of your home town and of one place you would like to visit.
lessons.send: Provide a map with a lat/long grid and example answers. EAL: pre-teach meridian with the orange picture. Stretch: use degrees and minutes to give more accurate coordinates.

lessons.title: Time zones around the world
objectives: Explain why the world has time zones
Calculate the time in another place using the time difference
Link time zones to longitude and the Prime Meridian

keywords.def: an area of the world that uses the same standard time
Greenwich Mean Time, the time on the Prime Meridian
the spinning of the Earth on its axis once every 24 hours
the number of hours between the time in two places

starter: Say Bismillah. Which line of longitude is 0°?
Does the Sun rise in the east or the west?

teach.heading: Why do we have time zones?
bullets: The Earth spins once every 24 hours.
The Sun reaches different places at different times.
When it is noon in one place, it is night elsewhere.
teach.note: Use a torch and a globe to show day and night. Ask: when it is lunchtime in London, is it day or night in Sydney? Night. Many pupils think the Sun moves; correct this: the Earth spins. This also affects salah times, which depend on the position of the Sun.

teach.heading: 15 degrees an hour
bullets: So every 15° of longitude is about one hour.
teach.note: Work through the division on the board. Link to longitude: moving 15° east means the Sun reaches you an hour earlier, so your clock is one hour ahead. Moving 15° west means it is one hour behind. 'East is ahead, west is behind' is a good phrase.

teach.heading: Working out time differences
bullets: GMT is the time at 0° longitude.
In November: Riyadh is GMT +3, Cairo is GMT +2, Lagos is GMT +1.
New York is GMT -5. Tokyo is GMT +9.
teach.note: Note that countries choose their own time zones for convenience and many use daylight saving. In November the UK is on GMT. Saudi Arabia is always UTC+3. Egypt is on UTC+2 in winter. The US East Coast is UTC-5 after daylight saving ends on 1 November 2026. Model: noon in London is 3 pm in Makkah.

teach.heading: Worked example
bullets: Makkah is +3 hours, so it is 13:00.
New York is -5 hours, so it is 05:00.
teach.note: Use a number line or clock faces. Do the Makkah example together, then ask pupils to calculate for Tokyo (+9 = 19:00). Common error: pupils subtract when they should add. Remind them 'east is ahead, so add'. Ask why we should check time before calling family abroad.

practice: It is 12:00 noon in London. What time is it in Makkah, Lagos and Tokyo?
It is 18:00 in Riyadh. What time is it in London?
independent: Complete a time-zone table for eight cities when it is 09:00 in London.
Plan a call between London and New York that suits both families (not at night).
Stretch: a plane leaves London at 08:00 and takes 7 hours to reach New York. Find the local arrival time.
exit: How many degrees of longitude is one hour of time?
When it is 10:00 in London, what time is it in Cairo in November?
lessons.homework: Ask a relative abroad what time it is for them now and calculate the time difference from London.
lessons.send: Provide a time-zone number line and a table to fill. EAL: practise 'ahead' and 'behind' with gestures. Stretch: explain why China uses one time zone even though it is very wide.

lessons.title: Ordnance Survey maps: symbols and six-figure grid references
objectives: Use eight points of the compass
Read four-figure and six-figure grid references
Recognise common Ordnance Survey symbols and use a key

keywords.def: the organisation that makes detailed maps of Great Britain
a set of numbers that gives the position of a place on a map
the number along the bottom (west to east) of a map
the number up the side (south to north) of a map
the relationship between distance on a map and distance on the ground

starter: Say Bismillah. How many degrees of longitude equal one hour of time?
When it is 10:00 in London, what time is it in Makkah?

teach.heading: Eight points of the compass
bullets: North, east, south, west and in between.
teach.note: Recap four points and add the four in-between ones. Practise by asking pupils to stand and face north-east. A compass rose should be on screen. Remind pupils that Muslims use direction to find the qibla, which is the direction of the Kaaba in Makkah.

teach.heading: Four-figure grid references
bullets: Along the corridor, then up the stairs.
Read the easting first, then the northing.
A four-figure reference names one grid square.
teach.note: Use the phrase 'along the corridor and up the stairs'. Model with an OS extract: find the vertical line numbered 12, then the horizontal line numbered 34, so the square to the right of and above their crossing is 1234. Misconception: pupils use the number to the right or above, but the reference is for the bottom-left corner of the square.

teach.heading: Six-figure grid references
bullets: Divide each grid square into ten parts.
The third and sixth digits are tenths.
A six-figure reference gives a precise point.
teach.note: Take square 1234 and divide it into tenths in both directions. A church at 4 tenths along and 7 tenths up becomes 124347. Practise with a grid on screen. Provide a plastic ruler or a grid overlay (on screen or paper) for accurate reading.

teach.heading: OS symbols and scale
bullets: Blue: water. Green: forests and parks. Brown: contour lines.
Symbols: church, post office, campsite, picnic site.
1:25,000 means 1 cm on the map is 250 m on the ground.
teach.note: Show an OS key. Pupils match symbols to meanings. For scale, 4 cm on a 1:25,000 map is 1 km. Many pupils find scale difficult; give a simple practice: if two points are 6 cm apart, the real distance is 1.5 km.

practice: Give the four-figure grid reference for the square containing the school.
Find the six-figure reference for the church in an OS extract.
independent: Complete the OS skills worksheet: compass directions, grid references, symbols.
Plan a walking route between two points using compass directions and distances.
Stretch: describe the route from the car park to the viewpoint using directions and grid references.
exit: Which number do you read first in a grid reference?
lessons.homework: Use a digital map to find your street and try writing an eight-direction route to the nearest park.
lessons.send: Provide a grid overlay and a step-by-step grid reference checklist. EAL: use the corridor and stairs gesture. Stretch: introduce contour lines and ask which route is steeper.

lessons.title: Where are the poles?
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is the Arctic an ocean but Antarctica a continent?
objectives: To understand where the Arctic and Antarctic are and how they differ
successCriteria: All: locate the Arctic and Antarctica on a globe
Most: describe two differences between the Arctic and Antarctica
Some: name countries that have land inside the Arctic Circle
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at creatures made for their habitats

keywords.def: the area around the North Pole: a frozen ocean surrounded by land
the continent around the South Pole
the most northern or southern point on Earth
a line of latitude at about 66.5°N
a huge, thick layer of ice covering land

hook.text: Polar bears and penguins never meet in the wild. Why not?

islamicLink.text: Allah made the earth with hot lands and frozen lands, and every creature suited to its home. Allah says: 'And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and the creatures He has spread through them' (ash-Shura 42:29). Polar bears and penguins are perfectly made for the cold.

starter.a: Around the globe, east to west
options: Around the globe, east to west

teach.heading: Two poles
teach.note: Spin a globe and point to the top and bottom.

teach.heading: The Arctic
teach.note: About four million people live in the Arctic, in countries such as Canada, Greenland (Denmark), Norway and Russia.

teach.heading: Antarctica
bullets: A continent covered by an ice sheet
No one lives there all year
teach.note: About 98% of Antarctica is covered in ice.

teach.heading: Arctic or Antarctic?
teach.note: Pupils call letters and numbers.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Where do penguins live in the wild?
options: Mainly Antarctica and the southern half of the world
check.why: Wild penguins live in the southern hemisphere; polar bears live in the Arctic.

practice.q: Is the North Pole on land or on ice over the sea?
practice.a: On sea ice over the Arctic Ocean
practice.model:
Look at the globe.
The North Pole is in the middle of the Arctic Ocean.
So it is on floating sea ice.

practice.q: Name two countries with land in the Arctic.
practice.a: For example: Canada and Norway

practice.q: Does anyone live in Antarctica all year?
practice.a: No: only scientists and staff visit

independent.q: Core: On two polar maps, label the North Pole, Arctic Ocean, Greenland, Canada, Russia, the South Pole, Antarctica and the Southern Ocean.
independent.a: All eight correctly placed on the right map
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: on the Arctic map, the centre is the North Pole; the big island near Canada is Greenland.

independent.q: Extend: Write two differences between the Arctic and Antarctica.
independent.a: The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by land; Antarctica is a continent surrounded by ocean. People live in the Arctic; no one lives in Antarctica all year.

independent.q: Stretch: Why is Antarctica colder than the Arctic?
independent.a: It is high land covered in thick ice; the Arctic Ocean water underneath keeps the Arctic a little warmer

exit.q: Antarctica is a:
exit.a: Continent

exit.q: Big question: why is the Arctic an ocean but Antarctica a continent?
exit.a: The Arctic is frozen sea around the North Pole surrounded by land; Antarctica is land covered by an ice sheet surrounded by sea

lessons.homework: Make a 'polar bear or penguin?' quiz of five facts for your family.
lessons.send: SEND: polar maps with dots to label from a word bank. EAL: north, south, ice, ocean. Stretch: find the Arctic Circle and Antarctic Circle on the globe.

lessons.title: Polar climate: cold, dark and dry
lessons.bigQuestion: How do people pray when the sun does not set for weeks?
objectives: To understand why the polar regions are so cold and have long days and nights
successCriteria: All: describe the polar climate
Most: explain why the poles are cold using the sun's angle
Some: explain polar day and polar night
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: light and the Earth's tilt
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: keeping prayer wherever we live

keywords.def: the usual weather of a place over many years
when the sun does not set for 24 hours or more
when the sun does not rise for 24 hours or more
how far north or south of the Equator
a place with very little rain or snow

hook.text: Is Antarctica a desert? Think about how much snow falls.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet, peace be upon him, told of a time when a day would be as long as a year, and said: 'Estimate its measure' for prayer (Sahih Muslim). Scholars use this to guide Muslims near the poles, where the sun may not set or rise for days, so that they still pray five times a day.

starter.q: At what latitude is the North Pole?

teach.heading: Why so cold?
bullets: Sunlight hits at a low angle
Its energy spreads over a bigger area
teach.note: Shine a torch straight down, then at a slant: the slanted light is spread out and weaker.

teach.heading: Record cold
teach.note: Compare a home freezer at about -18 °C.

teach.heading: A cold desert
bullets: Very little snow falls each year
The snow that falls rarely melts
teach.note: Desert means little rain or snow, not hot sand.

teach.heading: Polar day and night
teach.note: Inside the Arctic Circle there is at least one day a year when the sun does not set, and one when it does not rise.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Why is Antarctica called a desert?
options: Very little snow or rain falls
check.why: A desert is defined by low rain or snow, not heat.

practice.q: Why does slanted sunlight warm the ground less?
practice.a: Its energy is spread over a bigger area
practice.model:
Torch straight down: small bright circle.
Torch slanted: big dim patch.
Same energy, bigger area, so less warming.

practice.q: What was the coldest temperature recorded at Vostok?
What is polar night?
practice.a: When the sun does not rise for 24 hours or more

independent.q: Core: Write a polar climate fact box with four facts (temperature, rain or snow, day and night, wind).
independent.a: For example: down to -89.2 °C; very little snow; polar day and night; strong winds
independent.model: Teacher shows fact 1: 'Temperature: Antarctica can reach -89.2 °C, the coldest ever recorded.'

independent.q: Extend: Explain why the poles are cold, using the torch idea.
independent.a: Sunlight arrives at a low angle, so its energy is spread out; ice also reflects sunlight

independent.q: Stretch: How do Muslims living far north work out prayer times in summer when it hardly gets dark?
independent.a: Scholars give rulings to estimate times, for example by following the times of a nearer place or a fixed pattern

exit.q: Polar day means the sun:
exit.a: Does not set

exit.q: Big question: how do people pray when the sun does not set for weeks?
exit.a: Scholars advise estimating prayer times, for example from a nearby place, as the Prophet taught for days of unusual length

lessons.homework: Do the torch test at home with an adult and write what you notice.
lessons.send: SEND: climate fact box with picture prompts. EAL: cold, dark, light, wind. Stretch: find sunrise and sunset times today in Tromso, Norway.

lessons.title: How icebergs form
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is only the 'tip of the iceberg' visible?
objectives: To understand how icebergs form and why most of an iceberg is underwater
successCriteria: All: say what an iceberg is
Most: explain how icebergs break off glaciers and ice shelves
Some: explain why about nine-tenths of an iceberg is underwater
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at water in its forms

keywords.def: a large piece of freshwater ice floating in the sea
a slow river of ice
a thick floating sheet of ice joined to land
when ice breaks off a glacier or ice shelf
stay on top of water

hook.text: If you put an ice cube in a glass of water, how much of it sticks out? Try it!

islamicLink.text: Allah sends down from the sky mountains of cloud with hail in them (an-Nur 24:43). The ice of the poles holds most of the world's fresh water. Water, frozen or flowing, is one of Allah's great gifts.

starter.q: Polar night means the sun does not:

starter.a: Sunlight arrives at a low angle and ice reflects it

teach.heading: From snow to iceberg
bullets: Snow builds up and squashes into ice
Glaciers flow slowly to the sea
teach.note: This takes many years.

teach.heading: Icebergs and sea ice
bullets: Icebergs: from land ice, fresh water
teach.note: Many Arctic icebergs come from Greenland's glaciers.

teach.heading: The hidden part
bullets: Ice is a little lighter than sea water
teach.note: Use the ice cube in a glass to show it.

teach.heading: Why icebergs are dangerous
teach.note: This leads to next lesson: the Titanic.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: About how much of an iceberg is underwater?
check.why: About nine-tenths is underwater, which is why icebergs are so dangerous.

practice.q: An iceberg is 20 m above the water. Roughly how much is hidden if 10% shows?
practice.a: About 180 m below (the whole is about 200 m)

practice.q: What is calving?
practice.a: When ice breaks off a glacier or ice shelf

practice.q: Is an iceberg made of fresh or salt water?
practice.a: Fresh water

independent.q: Core: Draw a labelled diagram of an iceberg forming, from snow to a floating iceberg, with the water line.
independent.a: Snow, glacier, calving, iceberg with about 90% below the water line
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: a glacier reaching the sea, a piece breaking off, then a floating iceberg with a small top and large hidden part.

independent.q: Extend: Explain the difference between an iceberg and sea ice.
independent.a: Icebergs break off land ice and are fresh water; sea ice is frozen sea water

independent.q: Stretch: What does the saying 'the tip of the iceberg' mean in everyday speech?
independent.a: We can only see a small part of a much bigger problem

exit.q: Icebergs break off:
exit.a: Glaciers and ice shelves

exit.q: Big question: why is only the 'tip of the iceberg' visible?
exit.a: Ice is slightly lighter than sea water, so it floats with about 90% under the surface

lessons.homework: Freeze water in a small tub, float it in a bowl and estimate how much sticks out.
lessons.send: SEND: diagram with labels to place. EAL: snow, ice, break, float. Stretch: research the largest iceberg ever recorded.

lessons.title: Mapping a route across Antarctica
